extracted.intended_audience: graduate students and researchers learning/proving facts in algebraic geometry (readers of Vakil's 'The Rising Sea')
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts of a textbook chapter giving precise criteria/definitions and proof strategies for ampleness (Nakai‑Moishezon, Kleiman) and for modules/sheaves of differentials, with exercises and examples. Useful as a reference for proving or applying these theorems in algebraic-geometry work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nakai‑Moishezon criterion for ampleness
rubrics_metrics.description: If L is an invertible sheaf on a projective k-scheme X, and for every irreducible subvariety Y of X, (L^{dim Y} · Y) > 0, then L is ample.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statement is presented as a characterization of ampleness. Remarks: X need only be proper for the result (citations given). The proof is carried out by reductions (integral X, induction on dimension), showing high powers have sections, proving global generation off an effective divisor and then applying a curve-positivity criterion. Use Exercises and Serre vanishing in the proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ampleness is a numerical property
rubrics_metrics.description: (L^{dim Y} · Y) depends only on the numerical equivalence class of L, so ampleness depends only on the numerical equivalence class of L.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequences: ampleness makes sense on the N^1(X) vector space; ample Q-line bundles form a cone (ample cone) in N^1_Q(X). Cited propositions/exercises establish that the tensor product of ample sheaves is ample and that ample Q-line bundles form a cone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and openness of the ample cone
rubrics_metrics.description: The ample Q-line bundles in N^1_Q(X) form the ample cone of X. Proposition: If X is projective, the ample cone is open.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof sketch: choose a basis of N^1(X), express a given ample bundle as sums with small coefficients of basis classes coming from very ample bundles; small perturbations remain ample. Use Exercise references (very ample multiples, cone properties).

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof reductions for ampleness (strategy)
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove ampleness from intersection positivity: reduce to X integral (Exercises 18.8.A/B), work by induction on dimension, assume L is ample on any proper closed subvariety; base case dim 1 handled elsewhere.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the standard induction framework used in the textbook proof of Nakai‑Moishezon: make initial reductions to simplify the problem before cohomological/vanishing arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: High powers of L have sections (asymptotic cohomology growth)
rubrics_metrics.description: For L satisfying the hypotheses, sufficiently high tensor powers L^{⊗ m} have nonzero global sections (H^0(X, L^{⊗ m}) ≠ 0 for m ≫ 0); higher cohomology stabilizes/vanishes for large m.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Asymptotic Riemann–Roch to see χ grows like (m^n (L^n) / n!) + …, express L as difference of very ample bundles and apply long exact sequences plus Serre vanishing and the inductive hypothesis on subvarieties to conclude h^0>0 for m≫0.

rubrics_metrics.name: Global generation off an effective divisor and control of base locus
rubrics_metrics.description: If D is an effective divisor given by a section of a large power of L, then L^{⊗ m} is globally generated on the complement of D (any base locus is contained in D). For m large, restriction maps H^0(X, L^{⊗ m}) → H^0(D, L^{⊗ m}|_D) are surjective, enabling vanishing of base points on D as well.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use short exact sequences relating L^{⊗ m-1}, L^{⊗ m}, and their restrictions to divisors, cohomology long exact sequences, stabilization of H^1 for large m, Serre vanishing, and induction on dimension (ampleness on D) to deduce surjectivity and hence base-point-freeness for large m.

rubrics_metrics.name: From base-point-free + curve-positivity to ampleness
rubrics_metrics.description: If L (or a power) is base-point-free and has positive degree on every curve, then L is ample (referenced: Exercise 18.4.M).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the concluding criterion used in the proof of Nakai‑Moishezon: once L is base-point-free and intersects each curve positively, earlier exercises show L is ample.

rubrics_metrics.name: Kleiman’s theorem (nef positivity on subvarieties)
rubrics_metrics.description: If L is a nef invertible sheaf on a projective k-scheme X, then (L^{k} · V) ≥ 0 for every irreducible subvariety V ⊂ X of dimension k.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is stated as key to Kleiman’s numerical criterion; the theorem extends to proper case with citations. The proof is postponed until consequences are considered; it is used to relate nef and ample cones.

rubrics_metrics.name: Kleiman’s numerical criterion for ampleness
rubrics_metrics.description: (a) The nef cone is the closure of the ample cone. (b) The ample cone is the interior of the nef cone (for projective X).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Remarks: (a) follows because ample ⇒ nef and nef cone is closed; conversely, a nef class is the limit of ample classes. (b) uses openness of the ample cone and Exercise 20.4.B(b) showing small perturbations of a nef element by an ample class yield ampleness. Side remark: (a) fails if projective is relaxed to proper; interior may be empty for nonprojective varieties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit-of-ample and nef+ample facts (Exercise 20.4.B)
rubrics_metrics.description: (a) If L + εH is ample for all sufficiently small ε > 0 (H arbitrary), then L is nef. (b) If H is ample and L is nef then L + εH is ample for all sufficiently small ε > 0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hints: take limits ε→0 and apply Nakai‑Moishezon. These exercises connect the cones and are used in Kleiman's theorem arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof strategy for Kleiman’s theorem (polynomial P(t) approach)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reduce to irreducible reduced X and induct on dimension; fix a very ample H and consider P(t) = (L + tH)^n · X viewed as a polynomial in t. Show that if P(0) < 0 then P has positive real roots; analyze largest positive root t0 and use Nakai plus decomposition P = Q + R to deduce contradiction, concluding (L^n · X) ≥ 0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use positivity of (L+tH) for large t, Expansion of (L+tH)^{dim V} for subvarieties V, show Q(t0) ≥ 0 (via intersecting with very ample divisors to get effective curves) and R(t0) > 0 (Exercise 20.4.G) to force P(t0) > 0, contradiction. Exercises 20.4.D–20.4.G guide the details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Module of relative differentials Omega_{A/B} (defining properties)
rubrics_metrics.description: Ω_{A/B} is the A-module equipped with a map d: A → Ω_{A/B} satisfying (i) additivity d(a+a')=da+da', (ii) Leibniz d(aa') = a da' + a' da, and (iii) triviality on pullbacks db=0 for b in image of B.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This algebraic definition captures the notion of differentials; note d is B-linear (Exercise 21.2.A). Three equivalent constructions follow: explicit symbols modulo relations, universal property, and via presentations that sheafify well.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three constructions of Ω_{A/B}
rubrics_metrics.description: Ω_{A/B} may be constructed (i) concretely as A-linear combinations of symbols da modulo the rules (i)–(iii); (ii) by universal property as the universal B-linear derivation A → M; (iii) via presentations: if A = B[x_i]/(r_j) then Ω_{A/B} is generated by d x_i modulo relations d r_j = 0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The presentations viewpoint is practical for computations and sheafification. The universal property characterizes Ω_{A/B} uniquely and is useful conceptually; the concrete model is helpful for hands-on manipulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Key fact on generators and relations for Ω
rubrics_metrics.description: If A is generated as a B-algebra by elements x_i with relations r_j, then Ω_{A/B} is generated by the d x_i subject to the relations d r_j = 0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This allows computation of Ω from a finite presentation and explains why only generators and relations for the algebra are needed to compute differentials (see Exercise 21.2.D and conormal exact sequence for formal verifications).

rubrics_metrics.name: Finiteness properties of Ω (Proposition 21.2.4)
rubrics_metrics.description: If A is a finitely generated B-algebra, then Ω_{A/B} is a finitely generated A-module. If A is finitely presented over B, then Ω_{A/B} is finitely presented as an A-module.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Useful when working over Noetherian rings since finite type/presentation conditions simplify module-theoretic arguments and ensure coherence upon sheafification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examples: quotient and adding variables
rubrics_metrics.description: If A = B/I (quotient), then Ω_{A/B} = 0 (db = 0 for images of B). If A = B[x_1,...,x_n], then Ω_{A/B} = ⊕_i A dx_i (free of rank n).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Geometric intuition: localization/open subsets have no vertical differentials; affine n-space has trivial cotangent bundle of rank n. These building blocks suffice to understand general maps via standard constructions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Behavior on affine plane curves and relation to singularities
rubrics_metrics.description: For a plane curve A = k[x,y]/(f), Ω_{A/k} is free of rank 1 on the open D(∂f/∂x) and D(∂f/∂y); if Spec A is regular (nonsingular curve), these cover Spec A and Ω is invertible. If the curve is singular, Ω is not locally free (example y^2 = x^3 gives rank-2 fiber at origin).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compute relations (e.g., 2y dy = (3x^2-1) dx) to identify generators and vanishing loci of dx/dy; interpret vanishing as branching/tangent behavior geometrically. This shows Jacobian criterion links smoothness and local freeness of Ω.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jacobian description of Ω (21.2.E)
rubrics_metrics.description: If A = B[x_1,...,x_n]/(f_1,...,f_r), then Ω_{A/B} ≅ (⊕ A d x_i) / (⊕ A d f_j), i.e., can be viewed as the cokernel of the Jacobian matrix J: A^r → A^n.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practically compute Ω by taking the Jacobian matrix of relations; if J has full rank everywhere (smoothness), Ω is locally free. See Exercise 21.2.E and Jacobian-based consequences for fibers and smoothness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fiber of Ω at a rational point equals Zariski cotangent space
rubrics_metrics.description: If B is a k-algebra and m ⊂ B is a maximal ideal with residue field k, then Ω_{B/k} ⊗_B k ≅ m/m^2 (the cotangent space at that rational point).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This identifies algebraic differentials with geometric cotangent spaces; Corollary 21.3.8 generalizes this to separable residue field extensions. Use the Jacobian matrix to verify in coordinates (Exercise 21.2.F).

rubrics_metrics.name: Localization and base-change behavior of Ω
rubrics_metrics.description: Differentials behave well under localization: for multiplicative sets S, T as in Exercise 21.2.L, S^{-1}Ω_{A/B} ≅ Ω_{S^{-1}A/T^{-1}B}. For cartesian (tensor) diagrams A' ≅ B' ⊗_B A, there is a natural base-change map A' ⊗_A Ω_{A/B} → Ω_{A'/B'} which is an isomorphism in the co-Cartesian case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These properties justify sheafifying Ω and computing differentials locally; they accord with geometric intuition that open immersions induce no vertical differentials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cotangent exact sequence (affine version)
rubrics_metrics.description: For ring morphisms C → B → A there is a natural exact sequence of A-modules: A ⊗_B Ω_{B/C} → Ω_{A/C} → Ω_{A/B} → 0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Geometric interpretation: dual to the exact sequence of tangent sheaves 0 → T_{X/Y} → T_{X/Z} → π^* T_{Y/Z} → 0. The sequence need not be left-exact in general; left-exactness holds in sufficiently smooth situations (see later results and exercises).

rubrics_metrics.name: Conormal exact sequence (affine version)
rubrics_metrics.description: If B is a C-algebra and I ⊂ B with A = B/I, there is a natural exact sequence of A-modules: I/I^2 → A ⊗_B Ω_{B/C} → Ω_{A/C} → 0, where the first map δ sends i to 1⊗d i.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Geometric interpretation: dual to 0 → T_X → j^* T_Y → N_{X/Y} → 0; define the conormal sheaf N^∨_{X/Y} := I/I^2 and the normal sheaf as its dual. Exactness on the left fails in general but holds under smoothness hypotheses (see Theorem 21.3.6).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of conormal and normal sheaves
rubrics_metrics.description: For a closed embedding i: X ↪ Y cut out by ideal sheaf I, define the conormal sheaf N^∨_{X/Y} = I/I^2 (viewed as a quasicoherent sheaf on X). The normal sheaf is N_{X/Y} := Hom(N^∨_{X/Y}, O_X).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret I/I^2 as the sheaf of 'linear' relations cutting out X in Y; when the conormal is locally free the normal sheaf is its dual and corresponds to the classical normal bundle. Pay attention to subtleties: dualizing is not involutive in general unless reflexivity holds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regular embedding criterion for conormal/module freeness
rubrics_metrics.description: If A is Noetherian and I is generated by a regular sequence x_1,...,x_r then the natural map γ: (A/I)^⊕r → I/I^2 sending (a_1,...,a_r) ↦ Σ a_i x_i describes I/I^2 as a free (A/I)-module of rank r. Consequently, for a codimension-r regular embedding the conormal sheaf is locally free of rank r.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof reduces to localizing at primes and using properties of regular sequences; used to identify when conormal and hence normal sheaves are vector bundles (the 'good' geometric situation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Universal property of Ω (derivations representability)
rubrics_metrics.description: For A a B-algebra, Ω_{A/B} with d: A → Ω_{A/B} is characterized by the universal property: any B-linear derivation d' : A → M factors uniquely through d via an A-module map Ω_{A/B} → M.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the conceptual definition: Ω represents the functor of B-linear derivations. Use this viewpoint for abstract arguments and to prove functoriality (pullback) properties of Ω.
